description:
Every so often, I end up with a new gadget, accessory, or tool that’s so good that I wonder how I ever lived without it. My most recent example is this USB-C endoscope camera, which I snagged for just $17.

Also read: 14 nifty USB-C gadgets you didn’t know you needed
title: I use this $17 USB-C gadget every week, and I bet you don’t have one

description:
Augmental, a company that builds skinware (“body-coupled interfaces that let people control computers, communicate, and interact with AI without relying on their hands”), is now selling a tongue-controlled computer mouse called MouthPad.

The Bluetooth device is a specially designed pad that’s worn over the upper teeth. A pressure-sensitive control pad on the palate registers the user’s tongue movements, and those inputs are processed in conjunction with head tracking to control the mouse pointer, clicks, and scrolling. Each MouthPad is custom-made for each user, and all gestures can be customized via an accompanying app.
title: This $1,400 PC mouse is controlled entirely with your tongue

description:
ChatGPT maker OpenAI made a stir this week when it revealed that one of its most powerful AI models managed to sneak out of its confines for a joyride.

This unreleased model was supposed to stick to its sandbox as it ran a common online benchmark, reporting its findings to internal researchers on Slack when it was done.

Instead, the OpenAI model did something quite different. Confused by the benchmark’s instructions to post code publicly on GitHub, the model chose to break free, patiently probing its sandbox for weaknesses until it could carry out its orders.

That disclosure alone was enough to spook AI researchers, but
title: AI is learning to go rogue—and hack the system
